Abstract

Both studies were approved by the ethics committee at the least researcher's academic institution. All participants completed electronic informed consent before participating in the study.

The data analysis plan was pre-registered on Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/fg43m/?view_only=6a90c11ed10347c78d5471571f23f430 ).

Study materials (measures, data analysis codes, data) are available on OSF (https://osf.io/5pwhc/?view_only=d46e44085a1547c9b15a0abd792f9f7b ).

[div-01]

Public discourse frames screen time (i.e., time spent on digital devices) as inherently detrimental to well-being; yet research linking screen time to well-being is inconsistent and highly debated (Burnell et al., 2025; Ferguson et al., 2022; Størup & Lieberoth, 2023).

Moreover, adolescents report that the benefits of their smartphones outweigh the harms (Pew Research Center, 2024). These tensions between adolescent perceptions, public discourse, and equivocal research findings likely stem from a narrow focus on screen time quantity (i.e., time spent on screens, irrespective of what someone experiences) versus screen quality (i.e., the nature of subjective experiences during screen time, for example ranging from bad to good). That is, for some, 4 hours in screen time may facilitate mastery, social connections, and the pursuit of valued interests that enhance well-being whereas for others, it may increase feelings of incompetence, social isolation, or peer pressure that reduces well-being. Indeed, contexts that satisfy (versus frustrate) key needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness will differentiate when time spent in that context is related to well-being (Ryan & Deci, 2017). The overall purpose of this study is to explore psychological needs during screen time as quality indicators of screen time and their relationships with well-being beyond the contribution of screen time quantity (i.e., hours).

Limitations of Existing Research on Screen Time

Past research on the link between screen time and mental health (i.e., an umbrella term often used to describe indicators of well-and ill-being) has been criticized for small effects, narrow operationalizations of mental health, and a lack of research on user-centered experiences during screen time. Results from systematic reviews show little support for a robust relationship between screen time and mental health with overall effect sizes that may not be practically meaningful (e.g., g from |.02 to .22| between social media and mental health in Burnell et al., 2025; r = .06 for screens and mental health in Ferguson et al., 2022; r = .10 for screen time and depressive symptoms in Tang et al., 2021). Researchers are actively debating what constitutes a meaningful effect with some arguing small effects undermine causal claims (Ferguson, 2025) and others arguing small effects accumulate and are meaningful at the population level (Haidt & Rausch, 2026). Regardless of these debates, the small effect sizes from systematic reviews are likely masking heterogeneity in well-being derived from other factors such as subjective experiences during screen time.

Past research on screen time has focused extensively on markers of psychopathology (i.e., ill-being) rather than positive mental health (i.e., well-being) (Janicke-Bowles et al., 2023; Meier & Reinecke, 2021). Mental health is more than the absence of ill-being; rather, mental health exists along two separate continua of ill-being and well-being (Keyes, 2002). Someone who experiences anxiety can also experience positive affect or purpose in life. Meier and Reinecke (2021) found that most studies focused on ill-being, with few studies examining hedonic well-being (focusing on the affective components; feeling well) and even fewer on eudaimonic well-being (focusing on the flourishing components; doing well). Not examining both forms of well-being reduces our understanding of (1) why young adults value their screen time despite possible negative consequences and (2) how factors related to improved positive (or negative) screen time experiences impact their well-being. For example, it could be that young adults persist with high screen time because it affords opportunities to connect with others thereby improving affect (e.g., hedonic well-being) and enhancing meaning (e.g., eudaimonic well-being).

Finally, past research on screen time and well-being is limited by an over emphasis on a technology-centered assumption that it is the presence of time spent on screens itself (devoid of what someone experiences during that time) that impacts well-being (Meier & Reinecke, 2021).

Given the mixed findings between screen time and well-being, researchers examined if specific behaviours during screen time such as time spent being active (e.g., posting, commenting) or passive (e.g., scrolling) might better explain well-being. Nevertheless, in their review, Valkenburg and colleagues (2022) concluded that active or passive screen time remains too coarse of a measure to understand meaningful variation in well-and ill-being and produced mixed results (Valkenburg et al., 2022). Notably, examining active and passive screen time still relies on a technology-centred assumption because it does not account for how people experience and process their time. Knowing someone is engaging in active screen time does not tell us if that active screen time has positive (e.g., posting a picture reflecting a valued part of their identity) or negative (e.g., posting a picture that does not reflect their identity driven by external pressures) interactions and experiences. To this end, Meier and Reinecke, (2021) argued that researchers should include both technology-centred (e.g., screen time quantity) and user-centred approaches to better understand well-being. A user-centred approach sheds light on how a person processes their screen time (Meier & Reinecke, 2021) to better understand their attitudes, motivations, and experiences.

Quality of Screen Experiences from a Self-Determination Theory Perspective

One theory that can be used to understand the quality of screen experiences from a usercentred perspective is self-determination theory (SDT) (Rigby, 2023; Ryan & Deci, 2017). Deci and Ryan (2002) contend that humans have psychological needs for competence (i.e., to feel capable), autonomy (i.e., to feel volitional), and relatedness (i.e., to feel connectedness and belonging). These three psychological needs can be differentially satisfied or frustrated in any given context (e.g., sport, education, workplace), and their satisfaction (or frustration) will lead to enhanced (or undermined) well-being (Ryan & Deci, 2017). It is not the context (e.g., workplace, education) per se that imbues positive or negative outcomes, rather it is the degree to which people satisfy (or frustrate) their psychological needs within the context (Rigby, 2023).

From this perspective, if screens are just another context in which people live their lives (Odgers et al., 2020; Rigby, 2023), screen time experiences that offer opportunities to satisfy (versus frustrate) psychological needs (i.e., good quality experiences) should lead to enhanced wellbeing (Rigby, 2023; Ryan & Deci, 2017).

SDT has been used to understand quality of experiences in different screen time contexts. Przybylski et al. (2010) showed that video games can improve well-being in the short-term when players satisfy their psychological needs whereas frustration of those needs negatively influences well-being and enhances aggression. Similarly, social media can provide opportunities to satisfy and frustrate youths' psychological needs (West et al., 2024) that in turn impacts well-being and ill-being, respectively (Van de Casteele et al., 2023 Casteele et al., , 2024)). Interestingly, at the within-person level, the effect of screen time quantity on guilt, goal conflict, rumination, and negative affect was weakened if adolescents experienced higher need satisfaction during social media use (Van de Casteele et al., 2024). Overall, consistent with theory, psychological need satisfaction and frustration during screen time can serve as quality factors that are differentially related to wellbeing indicators.

Justification for the Present Study

When past research has examined psychological needs during screen time, it has narrowly focused on the quantity of time spent on different types of applications (i.e., social media, video games) or branded applications (e.g., Instagram) limiting conclusions about screen experiences beyond platform-specific experiences. In two studies using complementary methodologies, we examined relationships between overall screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration and well-being in university students. Notably, a core focus across studies was to examine psychometric properties and the best factor structure of responses to a measure modified to assess screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration, thereby providing evidence for a questionnaire to assess screen-related needs. Without evidence of score validity and reliability, inferences made about these variables could be meaningless. In the present study, we used two different research designs to assess (1) associations between needs and well-being beyond screen time quantity (cross-sectional design), thereby investigating if experiencing competence, autonomy, and relatedness during screen time is associated with well-being beyond the contribution of how long people spend on screens and (2) if screen-related needs predict daily hedonic and eudaimonic well-being (experience sampling design), allowing for an examining of dynamic, within-person processes that link screen-related needs to fluctuations in well-being at the daily level. Overall, the results will provide converging evidence about the role of need satisfaction and frustration during screen time as quality indicators of screen time and their relevance in enhancing our understanding of well-being.

We examined our research questions in university students. Roughly two thirds of university students do not meet current screen time guidelines (Weatherson et al., 2021) with device-logged data suggesting upwards of 6 hours per day on smartphones (Bradley et al., 2024).

Further, university students typically experience reductions in mental health during the first year of university (Barker et al., 2018). Therefore, with high screen time and lower mental health, university students represent a good population of interest to test theoretically meaningful links between quality indicators of screen time and well-being.

Open Science Statement and Ethics

The data analysis plan was pre-registered on Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/fg43m/?view_only=6a90c11ed10347c78d5471571f23f430). Study materials (measures, data analysis codes, data) are available on OSF (https://osf.io/5pwhc/?view_only=d46e44085a1547c9b15a0abd792f9f7b). For brevity, some details of the analytic plan are omitted herein, but are available at our OSF link. Deviations are noted herein. Both studies were approved by the university ethics board.

Study 1

To accurately assess quality of screen time, we examined the reliability and validity evidence for a modified need satisfaction and frustration scale (Chen et al., 2015). There is debate about the best factor structure for this scale that centres around two dimensional issues: (1) overlap among needs (e.g., competence, autonomy, and relatedness) and (2) whether satisfaction and frustration represent two distinct dimensions or one (Tóth-Király et al., 2018 , 2019).

First, the high interfactor correlations between needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness suggest that items designed to measure one factor (e.g., competence) unintentionally measure or load onto (i.e., cross-load) another factor (e.g., autonomy). Theoretically, each need overlaps (Ryan and Deci, 2017), but psychometrically, overlap makes it difficult to create unidimensional items. As such, constraining items to load onto a single factor can inflate interfactor correlations and bias parameter estimates (Tóth-Király et al., 2018). Second, high interfactor correlations between satisfaction and frustration dimensions suggest that there may be one underlying continuum representing global need fulfillment versus two continua representing distinct satisfaction and frustration dimensions (Tóth-Király et al., 2018).

To address these measurement issues, researchers have increasingly called for explicit analysis to (1) compare confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with no item cross-loadings to exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM that allows for items of one construct to crossload onto another construct) and (2) compare correlated factor models (i.e., separate unique latent variables) with bifactor models that allow researchers to specify both specific (i.e., competence, autonomy, relatedness) and global factors (i.e., global need fulfillment) (Holmquist et al., 2024; Tóth-Király et al., 2018). As such, we compared a six correlated factor model using CFA and ESEM and then evaluated a bifactor model (Objective 1.1). The models tested were guided by past research (Chen et al., 2015; Holmquist et al., 2024; Tóth-Király et al., 2018 , 2019). We also examined validity evidence based on relations to other variables to determine the expected pattern of convergent associations with well-being outcomes (Objective 1.2). Finally, we conducted a test of incremental validity to examine if screen-related psychological needs were associated with well-being indicators beyond the contribution of screen time duration (Objective1.3).

Objective 1.1: Examine the factor structure and reliability of scores from the modified screenrelated psychological need satisfaction and frustration scale (see Supplement 1, Figures S1-S3). Hypothesis 1.1a: We expected models that allowed cross-loadings (i.e., ESEM that permit items to load onto more than one factor) to represent the data better than models without crossloadings.

Hypothesis 1.1b: In the six correlated factors models (CFA and ESEM), the reliability will be good (> .60). In the bifactor models, global factor scores will have good reliability (> .60) and specific factor scores will have weaker reliability in line with past research (e.g. > .50; Tóth- Király et al., 2018).

Objective 1.2: Examine validity evidence based on convergence of the modified screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration scale.

Hypothesis 1.2: Screen-related psychological need satisfaction will be positively correlated with meaning, flourishing, and positive affect and negatively correlated with negative affect. Screenrelated psychological need frustration will be negatively correlated with meaning, flourishing, and positive affect and positively correlated with negative affect.

Objective 1.3: Examine if screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration is related to indicators of well-beingfoot_0 beyond the contribution of quantity of screen time.

Hypothesis 1.3: Higher screen-related psychological need satisfaction and lower need frustration will be independently related to more favourable well-being (i.e., higher meaning, flourishing, and positive affect; lower negative affect) regardless of quantity of screen time.

Study 1: Methods

Participants and Procedure

In the Fall of 2018, young adults from introductory psychology courses completed a onetime online questionnaire on Qualtrics for course credit or bonus credit. No a priori power analysis was calculated, but a goal of recruiting 500 participants was set to conduct latent variable analysis based on prior experience and general sample size guidelines. Eligibility criteria included being a student at the university, able to read and understand English, and 18 years of age or older.

Measures

Demographics. Participants reported their age, gender, population group (i.e., race/ethnicity), parents' marital status, and mother's and father's highest level of education completed.

Psychological need satisfaction and frustration.

The balanced 24-item measure of psychological need satisfaction and frustration (Chen et al., 2015) Screen Time. Two items from the International Sedentary Assessment Tool (Prince et al., 2017) were used to assess screen time in hours and minutes [one response option for their average on a typical weekday and one response option for a typical weekend day, separately. Item 1 asked about watching television or videos (e.g., DVDs, online videos) whereas item 2 asked about using a computer (e.g., PlayStation, tablet, smartphone, social networking tools). A manifest variable was created by adding the minutes reported in item 1 (tv and videos) and 2 (computers) and weighting it by time of the week [(weekday *5) + (weekend*2)]/7.

Eudaimonic Well-being:

The 8-item flourishing scale (Diener et al., 2010) assessed psychological flourishing. Items were rated on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). An example item is "I lead a purposeful and meaningful life". The 4-item meaning scale (Huta & Ryan, 2010) was used to assess meaning in life. Items were rated on a scale of 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much). An example item is "to what degree do you feel that your activity and experiences are meaningful".

Hedonic well-being:

The 10-item short-Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Mackinnon et al., 1999; Watson et al., 1988) was used to asses positive and negative affect. Items were rated on a scale of 1 (very slightly or not at all) to 5 (extremely). Example items included "scared" (negative affect) and "excited" (positive affect).

Data analysis

Detailed data cleaning and analysis plans, data, and code are available on OSF.

Data analysis for Objective 1.1

CFA models were estimated in Mplus 8 using robust full information maximum likelihood estimation, setting the variance of the latent variables to 1, and not allowing item cross-loadings or residual covariances. ESEMs were estimated with target rotation specifying that each item was allowed to load freely on its respective latent factor whereas cross-loadings were permitted but specified to be as close to zero as possible (See Supplement 1, Figures S1 to S3 for each possible structure). All items were treated as continuous and participants with incomplete data were retained. Composite reliability (omega) was calculated for the latent variables of each model.

Comparing the factor structures. We performed two stepsfoot_1 that each involved consideration of goodness-of-fit statistics, parameter estimates, reliability, and theory. Specifically:

Step 1. Compare the six correlated factors model using CFA and ESEM specifications (see Figure S1, Models 1 and 2 in Supplement 1) to examine if the addition of item cross-loadings should be incorporated into the factor structure (Morin et al., 2020; Tóth-Király et al., 2018).

Goodness-of-fit was interpreted with values close to comparative fit index (CFI) > .95 and root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) < .06 indicative of good model fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999). Chi-square values are presented but not interpreted given their sensitivity to large sample sizes. The ESEM model was selected as superior to the CFA model only if the following criteria (Morin et al., 2020) were met and reliability for the latent factors was acceptable (latent factor reliability > .60): a. Improved goodness-of-fit statistics (i.e., higher CFI and lower RMSEA values that meet or exceed the thresholds noted above). b. Smaller latent factor correlations. Based on past research (Tóth-Király et al., 2018), the latent factor correlations should be reduced (on average) by at least .15 to be considered meaningful. The interfactor correlations should remain theoretically aligned. c. Small-to-moderate cross-loadings or large cross-loadings that could make conceptual sense. We defined small-to-moderate cross-loadings as standardized loadings < .40.

For a large cross-loading (i.e., > .40) to make conceptual sense, it had to clearly contain elements of a different psychological need in the wording. Morin et al., (2020) argued that if there are multiple moderate-to-large cross-loadings, it may suggest the presence of an unmodeled global factor. As such, if moderate-to-large cross-loadings were found in the ESEM model, it was not ruled out based solely on this criterion (rather, criteria a, b, and d would be considered). d. Latent factors were well defined. We interpreted well defined as having > 75% of the standardized target factor loadings for a latent factor being > .50.

Step 2: Using the final model selected in step one, we examined two bifactor structures shown in Figure S2 (model 3 or 4) and S3 (models 5 or 6) in Supplement 1. To examine if the bifactor models were superior to a six correlated factor model, we followed recommendations by Morin et al., (2020) and ensured reliability for the latent factors was acceptable (global latent factor reliability > .60 and specific latent factors reliability > .50): a. Improved goodness-of-fit statistics (as noted above). b. A well-defined global factor. We interpreted well defined global factors as having > 75% of the standardized factor loadings for the global latent factor > .50. c. Some reasonably well-defined specific factors. Here, it is not essential for all specific factors to be well defined (Morin, 2020). For parsimony and theoretical alignment, we interpreted well defined specific factors as having the majority (i.e., 50% or 2 of 4 item loadings) of standardized target loadings > .50. If a specific factor failed this criterion, the bifactor model was rejected as it is difficult to theoretically interpret a solution where there is a global factor and only a few well-defined specific factors, given contentions in SDT about the uniqueness of each of the three psychological needs (see Holmquist et al., 2023).

Data analysis for Objective 1.2

SEM was used to estimate a model with all variables of interest to obtain correlations between screen-related psychological needs and well-being latent variables. First, three separate CFAs were estimated for each well-being indicator (meaning, flourishing, and positive and negative affect) to ensure data model fit, using the same criteria described above (details reported on OSF project page). Acceptably-fitting independent well-being models were added together into one overall well-being model. To examine error-free correlations (i.e., validity evidence based on relations to other variables), an overall measurement model was estimated by combining the well-being model with the screen-related psychological needs model.

Data analysis for Objective 1.3

Based on the final retained model used to examine objective 1.2, we estimated regression paths from well-being indicators onto screen-related psychological need variables and the composite variable of screen time quantity (see Figure S4 in Supplement 1). Finally, this model was repeated controlling for age, gender, parents' marital status, and mother's and father's education. Adjusted and unadjusted models were interpreted.

Exploratory Analysis (Incremental Validity)

To examine the incremental validity of screen-related psychological need variables as a group beyond the contribution of screen time quantity, the unadjusted SEM model was reestimated using procedures for testing incremental validity in SEM (Feng & Hancock, 2022; see details of analysis in Supplement 1 ). This analysis was not pre-registered but deemed relevant to understanding the unique effect of screen-related need experiences on well-being.

Inference Criteria and Effect Sizes

Unless noted otherwise above, inferences made from analyses described above were made based on p-values (p < .05) and 95% confidence intervals. The magnitude of the bivariate correlations was interpreted as small (.10), medium (.30), and large (.50). We interpreted R² as small (.01), medium (.09), and large (.25). The smallest effect sizes of interest (i.e., correlations > .10; Ferguson et al., 2021 and R² values > .04; Ferguson, 2016) were thresholds for describing whether effects were practically meaningful.

Study 1: Results

Descriptive statistics

Detailed demographic data, missing data, and descriptive statistics are presented in Supplement 1. Briefly, participants (N = 348, Mage = 19.56 years, SD = 2.49) ranged in age from 18 to 37, were mostly female (74.1%) followed by male (25.6%) or other (.3%). The majority had parents who were married (60.9%) followed by divorced (22.3%). The most frequently reported highest level of education for their mother was a bachelor's degree (31.9%) and for their father was a Diploma or 1-3 years of college (27.6%). They self-reported an average of 8.13 hours (SD = 4.30) on screen time per day. Missing data ranged from 0.9 to 3.4% on items from well-being scales and was 2.9% on screen time duration.

Hypothesis 1.1: Factor Structure of Screen-related Psychological Needs Scale

Examining the six correlated factors models, both CFA and ESEM models had good fit indices (see Table 1 and Supplement 1 Tables S.3-S.4 for factor loadings, latent variable correlations, omegas). The ESEM model demonstrated improved goodness-of-fit indices compared to the CFA model (i.e., criterion 'a' was met). Latent variable correlations were theoretically aligned (valence and direction) and associations were reduced in the ESEM model (r range = |.04 to .59|) compared to the CFA model (r range = |.04 to .62|); however, the reduction in magnitude was not considered substantial (reduction range = .002-.08; Mreduction = 0.03) and therefore criterion 'b' was not met. Cross-loadings in the ESEM model were all below the smallto-moderate threshold of .40 (all < .37) and all latent factors were well defined by their target loading (λ > .44; therefore criterion 'c' was met). All latent factors were well defined with 75% or more items above .50 in the CFA model (λ range = .59-.93) and the ESEM model (λ range = .48-.92; therefore criterion 'd' was met). Reliability was good in both models (omega > .80).

Overall, since only 3 of the 4 criteria for retaining the ESEM model over the CFA model were met, the six correlated factor CFA model was retained as the base structure before testing bifactor modelsfoot_2 . Goodness-of-fit did not improve in the CFA bifactor specifications compared to the six correlated factor model (see Table 1; see Supplement 1 tables S.5-S.6 for factor loadings, latent variable correlations, omegas; criterion 'a' was not met). Neither the one nor two global factor models had well defined global factors (λ range = .27-.79; no factors had more than 68% of items with loadings > .50; criterion 'b' was not met). The specific factors of both CFA bifactor models were well defined (> 50% of loadings per specific factor being > .50) except for competence frustration in the two global factor model (criterion 'c' was met). Finally, reliability of the global factor(s) and specific factors was good (omega > .73). Therefore, since only 1 of the 3 criteria were met for retaining a bifactor model, the six correlated factor CFA model was selected as the final model.

Hypothesis 1.2: Validity evidence of convergence

Results of the CFAs for the well-being measures are presented in Table 1 (see model specification details in Supplement 1). The overall measurement model fit the data although CFI was slightly low (ꭓ 2 (942) = 1585.40, p < .001; CFI = .93, RMSEA = .04, 90% CI [.04, .05]). Supporting hypothesis 1.2, bivariate correlations (see Table 2) between latent variables indicated that screen-related need satisfaction was positively correlated with positively valenced indicators of well-being with a medium-to-large effect size (r range = .35-.71) and negatively correlated with negative affect with a small-to-medium effect size (r range = -.21 to -.44). Conversely, screen-related need frustration was positively correlated with negative affect with a medium-tolarge effect size (r range = .32 to .61) and negatively correlated with positively valanced wellbeing indicators with a small-to-large effect size (r range = -.18 to -.63). All significant correlations were above the threshold for smallest effect size of interest.

Hypothesis 1.3: Screen-related needs related to well-being indicators beyond screen time quantity

The SEM provided a satisfactory fit to the data (unadjusted: n = 338, ꭓ 2 (984) = 1634.63, p < .001, CFI = .93, RMSEA = .04, 90% CI [.04, .05] see Table 3). Partially supporting hypothesis 1.3, higher screen-related competence and autonomy satisfaction were significantly related to higher flourishing, meaning, and positive affect. Higher screen-related relatedness satisfaction was related to higher flourishing. Contrary to hypothesis, higher screen-related psychological need frustration was not significantly related to flourishing, meaning, or positive affect, but consistent with hypotheses higher competence frustration and autonomy frustration were related to higher negative affect. Screen time quantity was unrelated to any well-being indicator. The overall model effects were deemed large based on R² (range = .29 to .67). This model was repeated by adding regression paths from well-being indicators to the covariates of age, gender, parents' marital status, mother's education, and father's education (adjusted: n = 328, ꭓ 2 (1194) = 1868.94, p < .001, CFI = .92, RMSEA = .04, 90% CI [.04, .05]foot_3 . The pattern of the results was the same for regression paths and similar for R² values (Table 3).

Exploratory Analysis (Incremental Validity)

As a group, screen-related psychological needs accounted for a large unique proportion of the variance in well-being (meaning = 32%, flourishing = 67%, positive affect = 26%, negative affect = 27%) beyond that accounted for by screen time quantity (0.2% to 0.5%; see Supplement 1 for detailed results).

Sensitivity analysis with outliers

Although not pre-registered, as a sensitivity analysis, we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate procedure to the unadjusted SEM results to rule out Type I error inflation.

The family of tests was defined within each outcome (i.e., across predictors for each well-being indicator). The general pattern of results remained consistent, particularly for competence satisfaction whereas an effect associated with autonomy satisfaction and positive affect became non-significant (see Table 3). In another sensitivity analysis, the final unadjusted and adjusted models were re-estimated including all participants (N = 358) regardless of their outlier (z > 3.29) status on screen time quantityfoot_4 . The pattern of results based on direction and statistical significance was identical between models (see Supplement 1, Table S.7).

Study 1: Brief Discussion

Overall, the modified scale to assess screen-related psychological needs demonstrated good reliability and validity (based on factor structure and relations in expected directions with convergent and divergent well-being measures). The data fit six correlated factors representing each psychological need (competence, autonomy, and relatedness) for each valence (satisfaction and frustration) with no cross-loadings. Hypotheses were generally supported in that competence and autonomy satisfaction were related to positive indicators of well-being (but not negative affect) whereas competence and autonomy frustration were related to negative affect (but not positive indicators of well-being). Relatedness satisfaction was related to flourishing only. These findings were considered practically meaningful based on effect sizes and were beyond the contribution of screen time quantity suggesting screen-related needs can be assessed validly and could be good indicators of positive and negative quality screen time experiences.

Study 2 Brief overview

Study 1 provided cross-sectional evidence supporting the validity and reliability of our modified measure of screen-related need satisfaction and that screen-related needs could represent quality indicators of screen time that differentially relate to well-being. Nonetheless, those findings require replication and extension across time and levels of analysis. Therefore, the first purpose of Study 2 was to replicate the psychometric properties and pattern of relationships between screen-related needs and well-being beyond the contribution of screen time quantity.

Replicating these results would suggest robust between-person relationships but would not indicate whether these associations operate within individuals over time. To this end, screenrelated need experiences likely fluctuate moment-to-moment and at different points in the day. Ryan et al., (2010) found that well-being was higher during non-work time and weekends because people are better able to fulfill their psychological needs during leisure time. Therefore, for students where evenings tend to be more self-directed, evenings may provide a context with greater opportunity for need satisfying (versus frustrating) screen time experiences, and the association between needs and well-being may be stronger in the evening. Cross-sectional designs cannot capture these dynamic within-person processes. Therefore, the second purpose of Study 2 was to use an experience sampling design (ESM) to examine short-term temporal associations unfolding within individuals over time and to determine if links between needs and well-being are moderated by time of day (morning versus evening). Using an ESM design also minimizes recall bias and captures screen-related need experiences closer to when they occur.

Objective 2.1: To cross-validate the factor structure of the modified psychological need satisfaction and frustration scale found in Study 1.

Hypothesis 2.1: The final factor structure found in Study 1 will fit the data well and demonstrate good score reliability.

Objective 2.2: Examine if results from Study 1 Objective 1.3 (i.e., if screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration is related to indicators of well-being beyond the contribution of quantity of screen time) replicate. This objective is new and was not preregistered 6 . Hypothesis 2.2: Higher screen-related psychological need satisfaction and lower need frustration will be independently related to more favourable well-being (i.e., higher meaning, flourishing, and positive affect; lower negative affect) regardless of quantity of screen time.

Objective 2.2: Examine in the moment within-and between-person associations between screen-related psychological need satisfaction and well-being and if these associations differed by morning or evening assessments over seven days. 6 In our pre-registration we had an objective and hypothesis related to this question but including results from two surveys separated by 1 week. This objective and hypothesis was removed at the suggestion of an anonymous reviewer given the weak rationale that our general measures of well-being would capture change across one week. The results from the pre-registered change analysis are presented in Supplemental File 3. Hypothesis 2.2a (within-person effects): compared to their own average, if an individual has higher psychological need satisfaction during screen time, they will have more favourable than their average well-being (i.e., higher meaning and positive affect; lower negative affect) and these associations will be stronger in the evening.

Hypothesis 2.2b (between-person effects): on average, people who have higher psychological

need satisfaction during screen time will have more favourable well-being (i.e., higher meaning and positive affect; lower negative affect) and these associations will be stronger in the evening.

Study 2: Methods

Participants and Procedures

Data collection began in the Fall of 2020 and ended in winter 2021. Time 1 (day 1) was a full assessment with complete scales. Times 2-8 (days 2-8) were an experience sampling portion with twice daily (morning and evening) single-item assessments for seven days. All surveys were completed online using the ExpiWell app (ExpiWell, 2024) installed on participants' personal smartphones. Time 1 was completed on any day of the week after completing informed consent.

For Times 2-8, participants were randomly notified on their smartphone via ExpiWell twice per day (between 10AM-12PM and between 7-PM-9PM) and had 1 hour to complete the questionnaire. No a priori power analysis was conducted. Our goal of recruiting at least 250 participants with oversampling of ~500 was based on prior experience and available resources to conduct the study.

Participants (n = 645 at Time 1; n = 629 completed at least one daily survey across times 2-8) were university students > 17 years and were taking introductory psychology courses. They had to own a smartphone and be able to read and understand English. Participants could receive up to 1.50% course credit (or bonus credit) and up to a $20 (CAD) e-gift card based on how many surveys they completed (see Supplement 2 for details).

Measures

Time 1 Measures:

Screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration, screen time duration, and general well-being were measured as described in Study 1.

Time 2-8 Daily ESM Measures:

In the moment screen time use: Participants were first asked if they had used a screenbased device for leisure activity within the last hour (Yes/No). If they answered yes, they responded to screen-related needs and general well-being questions. If they answered no, they received no further questions until the next scheduled prompt. Well-being: One item from two well-being measures described above was used to assess meaning ("to what degree do you feel that your activity and experiences are meaningful"), positive affect ("enthusiastic"), and negative affect ("afraid") based on how participants felt in the moment. Items were selected because they had the strongest factor loadings in a factor analysis using data from Study 1 (see pre-registration for details). Single item indicators of wellbeing were the outcomes in each analysis.

Data analysis

Data analysis for Objective 2.1

Factor structures and reliability were estimated and interpreted for Time 1 responses of the full modified screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration scale following procedures described in Study 1.

Data analysis for Objective 2.2

Latent variables were modelled based on the best factor structure identified for screenrelated psychological needs in this sample. Well-being and screen time quantity were modeled using the same procedures as in Study 1. This analysis used Time 1 data only.

Exploratory analyses (Incremental Validity: Study 2)

As in Study 1, the unadjusted SEM from Objective 2.2 was re-estimated to examine incremental validity (Feng & Hancock, 2022; see details of analysis in Supplement 2). This analysis was not pre-registered but deemed relevant to understanding the unique effect of screenrelated need experiences on well-being and determine if Study 1 results replicated.

Data analysis for Objective 2.3

Multilevel linear models with repeated measures nested within persons were used to examine the associations between in the moment screen-related psychological need satisfaction and wellbeing outcomes and to test if these associations differed based on morning or evening assessments (Times 2-8). We used R software (R Core Team, 2018), RStudio (RStudio Team, 2020), packages lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), lmertest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017), and ggplot2 (Wickham, 2009). Psychological need satisfaction was person-mean centered to test withinperson effects. Person means of need satisfaction were added to test between-person effects. A dummy code representing time of day (morning = 0, evening = 1) was used to test its interaction with psychological need satisfaction. Finally, a dummy code accounting for weekend (Saturdays and Sundays) effects (weekend = 1, weekday = 0) was added. This model was re-estimated controlling for time 1 demographic information (age, gender, parents' marital status, mother's education, father's education). Significant interaction terms were probed with simple slopes. We attempted to estimate all intercepts and slopes as random given that there could be variation present; however, when the models would not converge, random slopes were tested one at a time. R² for adjusted and unadjusted models were calculated using the r2MLM package (Rights & Sterba, 2019).

Inference Criteria and Effect Size

Inference criteria for the SEM models were interpreted as noted in Study 1. Inferences for the multilevel models were made based on p-values (p < .05), using the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate procedure to correct for Type I error inflation due to multiple testing. This procedure defined the p-values within each well-being model as a family of tests for the purposes of correction (three models total). Effect sizes were interpreted for the unadjusted and adjusted models as outlined in Study 1.

Study 2: Results

Descriptive statistics

Detailed demographic data, missing data analysis, and descriptives are available in Supplement 2. Participants ranged in age from 16 to 58 (Mage = 20.34 years, SD = 4.79), identified as woman (80.1%), man (18.6%), other (0.9), or preferred not to answer (0.3%). The majority had parents who were married (59.2%) followed by divorced (20.3%). The most frequently reported highest level of education for their mother was a Diploma or 1-3 years of college (32.1%) and for their father was a Diploma or 1-3 years of college (27.5%). They selfreported an average of 9.10 hours (SD = 4.58) on screen time per day. Missing data on wellbeing items ranged from 0-3.7% at Time 1.

Hypothesis 2.1: Factor Structure of Screen-related Psychological Needs

Both CFA and ESEM models had good fit (see Table 4 and Supplement 2 Tables S.3-S.4).

The ESEM model demonstrated improved goodness-of-fit indices compared to the CFA model (i.e., criterion 'a' was met). Latent variable correlations were theoretically aligned (valence and direction) and were reduced in the ESEM model (r range = |.04 to .58|) compared to the CFA model (r range = |.04 to .61|); however, the reduction in magnitude was not considered substantial (reduction range = .002-.11; Mreduction = 0.04) and therefore criterion b was not met.

Cross-loadings in the ESEM model were all below the small-to-moderate threshold of .40 (all < .37) and all latent factors were well defined by their target loading (λ > .44; therefore criterion 'c' was met). All latent factors were well defined with 75% or more items above .50 in the CFA model (λ range = .59-.91) and the ESEM model (λ range = .44-.94; therefore criterion 'd' was met). Reliability was good in the CFA and ESEM models (omega > .75). Overall, since only 3 of the 4 criteria for retaining the ESEM model over the CFA model were achieved, the six correlated factors CFA model was retained as the base structure before testing bifactor modelsfoot_5.

Goodness-of-fit did not improve in the CFA bifactor specifications compared to the six correlated factor model (see Table 4 and Supplement 2 Tables S.5-S.6; criterion 'a' was not met).

Neither the one nor two global factor models had well defined global factors (λ range = .08-.63; no factors had more than 50% of items with loadings > .50; criterion 'b' was not met). The specific factors of both CFA bifactor models were well defined (> 50% of loadings per specific factor being > .50; criterion 'c' was met). Finally, reliability of the global factor(s) and specific factors was good (omega > .68). Overall, since only 1 of the 3 criteria were met for retaining a bifactor model, the six correlated factor CFA model was selected as the final model.

Hypothesis 2.2: Screen-related needs related to well-being indicators (Time 1 data)

Results of the CFAs for the well-being measures at T1 are presented in Table 4 (see Supplement 2 for details and for correlations). An overall measurement model was estimated with all latent variables at T1. This model provided a satisfactory fit to the data (ꭓ 2 (941) = 1845.73, p < .0 01, CFI = .93, RMSEA = .04, 90% CI [.036, .041]; see Supplemental File 2 Table S.9 for bivariate correlations). Next, regression paths were added from well-being latent factors to each latent variable representing screen-related psychological needs and a composite variable representing screen time quantity (in hours). This model provided a satisfactory fit to the data (unadjusted: n = 641, ꭓ 2 (982) = 1857.41, p < .001, CFI = .93, RMSEA = .04, 90% CI [.04, .04]; see Table 5). The pattern of results was generally the same for regression paths and R² increased when adjusting for covariates (R² change .01-03) (adjusted: n = 638; ꭓ 2 (1234) = 2275.09, p < .001, CFI = .92, RMSEA = .04, 90% CI [.03, .04]).

Study 2 partially replicated Study 1 results (see

Table 5 and Supplemental File 2 Table S.10 for a direct comparison between Study 1 and Study 2 of unadjusted effects). Competence satisfaction remained a significant correlate of well-being and autonomy and competence frustration remained significant correlates of negative affect. Failing to replicate, three (of nine) significant effects of autonomy satisfaction were not significant (p > .05) in Study 2. Additionally, of the 19 non-significant effects in Study 1, seven became statistically significant, particularly effects of competence frustration and relatedness frustration. Unexpectedly, autonomy frustration emerged as a significant positive correlate of meaning and flourishing in Study 2. The overall R² values were moderate-to-large, but smaller in magnitude compared to Study 1 (range = .23 to .49). Fully replicating Study 1, screen time quantity was not statistically significantly related to any well-being indicator.

Exploratory Analysis (Incremental Validity: Study 2)

As a group and replicating Study 1, screen-related psychological needs accounted for a moderate-to-large unique proportion of the variance in well-being (meaning = 21%, flourishing = 47%, positive affect = 21%, negative affect = 33%) beyond that accounted for by screen time quantity (0.5% to 1.8%; see Supplement 2 for detailed results).

Sensitivity analysis

Although not pre-registered, to replicate Study 1 and rule out Type I error inflation, we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate procedure to the SEM results at Time 1.

The general pattern of results remained consistent, particularly for competence satisfaction and frustration whereas three effects associated with autonomy frustration and relatedness frustration became non-significant (see Table 5). In another planned sensitivity analysis, the final unadjusted (N = 652) and adjusted models (N = 649) were re-estimated including all participants regardless of their outlier status on screen time quantity. The pattern of the results based on direction and statistical significance was identical between models except one effect (relatedness frustration and negative affect) crosses significance even though the estimate remains almost identical (see Supplement 2, Table S.11).

Hypothesis 2.2: Within-and between-person relationships

Unconditional models showed considerable within-and between-person variability in negative affect (ICC = .57), positive affect (ICC = .44), and meaning (ICC = .48). All models accordingly included a random intercept. Select models included additional random effects for within-person effects where model convergence could be achieved (see footnote in Table 6). Our hypotheses were generally supported. Participants who had higher screen-related psychological need satisfaction on average had more favourable general well-being (between-person; Table 6).

Additionally, on days when a participant's screen-related psychological need satisfaction was higher than usual, they reported better-than-usual general well-being (within-person). For positive affect, this effect was strongest in the evening (see Figure 1 in the Supplement 2 Figure S.1). Fixed effects for meaning and positive affect were medium and above the smallest effect size of interest (R² range = .15-.24) but small and bordering the smallest effect size of interest for negative affect (R² .03 and .05; see Table 6 for breakdown of R² values).

Study 2: Brief Discussion

Results from Study 2 largely replicated Study 1. The factor structure found was replicated (Hypothesis 2.1) and screen-related needs were associated with well-being beyond the effect of screen time duration (Hypothesis 2.2). Extending Study 1, at both within-and between-person levels of analysis, higher screen-related need satisfaction was associated with more favourable hedonic and eudaimonic well-being (Hypothesis 2.3), and this effect was stronger in the evening for positive affect.

General Discussion

Across two studies we found psychological need experiences during screen time were related to hedonic and eudaimonic well-being beyond the effect of screen time quantity. First, we found validity and reliability evidence for responses to a modified scale to assess screen-related psychological need satisfaction and frustration as six correlated factors. Second, across two studies, we found that screen-related psychological need satisfaction (particularly competence) was associated with positive well-being indicators whereas frustration (particularly competence and autonomy) was related to negative affect beyond the effect of screen time quantity (which was unrelated to well-being across all models). Finally, examining the daily data across one week, we found that people who have higher screen-related need satisfaction tend to have higher well-being overall, and in moments when one's screen-related need satisfaction is higher than typical for them so too was their well-being.

All effects were above the smallest effect size of interest (R² range .15 to .67) except in the daily study with negative affect as the outcome (R² .03 and .05 for unadjusted and adjusted models). Overall, university students can have positive or negative quality need experiences during screen time that are differentially related to feeling good (i.e., hedonic well-being) and doing well (eudaimonic well-being) beyond the effects of screen time quantity.

Measuring Quality Indicators of Screen Time

Across both studies, responses to the modified basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration scale (Chen et al., 2015) demonstrated evidence of validity and reliability. Notably, consistent with the original factor structure (Chen et al., 2015) and theory (Ryan & Deci, 2017), the best representation of the data was a six-correlated factor model representing each psychological need (i.e., competence, autonomy, and relatedness) as either satisfaction or frustration with no item cross-loadings. More complicated factor structures tested in this study (ESEM, bifactor models) did not show sufficiently large enough benefits such as reduced latent variable correlations. Any advantages associated with modelling combined (i.e., global) and unique (i.e., specific) effects would have come at the cost of increased model complexity requiring larger sample sizes, and potentially compromised meaning of latent variables. Our approach guided by past research (Morin et al., 2020; Tóth-Király et al., 2019) shows that specifying a priori criteria when determining the best model fit can help weigh the benefits against the costs of fitting increasingly complex models and help researchers avoid selecting models based solely on improved goodness-of-fit statistics. These findings require replication given that validation is ongoing process.

Quality and Quantity of Screen Time and Well-being

There was strong support for the finding that screen time quantity was not related to wellbeing in any model or sensitivity analysis when accounting for screen-related needs. In tests of incremental validity isolating the combination of screen-related needs from screen time duration, screen time duration accounted for virtually no variance in well-being outcomes. These findings support previous contentions (Odgers et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2021) and theoretical tenets (Ryan & Deci, 2017) that using time spent in screen contexts devoid of understanding what people are experiencing during that time is unlikely to help us understand the link between screen time and well-being. Our findings suggest that screen-related needs could represent a quality indicator of experiences during screen time that are differentially related to eudaimonic and hedonic wellbeing.

Regarding the specific effects of each screen-related psychological need, our crosssectional analyses across studies found strong support for a robust link between (1) screen-related competence satisfaction and well-being and (2) competence frustration and autonomy frustration and negative affect. Supporting the dual-process model in self-determination theory (Ryan & Deci, 2017), satisfaction variables were more robustly linked to positively valanced indicators of well-being compared to frustration variables that were more robustly linked to negative affect. In our analyses, these effects were present regardless of false discovery rate corrections, adjustment from covariates (except for positive affect in Study 1), and inclusion or omission of outliers. The robustness of competence is consistent with findings from video game and well-being research (Przybylski et al., 2010) suggesting feeling capable, effective, and competent while using screens is salient for hedonic and eudaimonic well-being.

Except the robust associations between competence and well-being indicators across studies, the effects of autonomy and relatedness with well-being were inconsistent. Researchers examining needs during social media use (Van de Casteele et al., 2023; see their supplemental analyses) and video gaming (Przybylski et al., 2010) have also noted that all three psychological needs were not consistently related to well-being indicators. According to theory, all three psychological needs are essential for well-being, but each need overlaps (Ryan & Deci, 2017).

This degree of overlap compromises the measurement of distinct needs. Whereas our bivariate correlations demonstrated that each need was associated with well-being indicators, when modelled simultaneously in the SEMs their shared variance attenuated relationships with wellbeing and in some cases created spurious findings in the opposite direction (see Study 2 autonomy frustration). An alternative explanation for why relatedness and autonomy were not consistently related to well-being could be due to measurement. Although items were modified to cue screen time, the content of the items may have been too vague to capture unique screen time manifestations of need experiences. For example, the item "during screen time I feel that my decisions reflect what I really want" (i.e., autonomy satisfaction) may be too vague and could be better contextualized to help readers understand what decisions are being made during screen time. More research examining validity evidence based on item content and response processes (i.e., how people interpret and respond to items) would be useful to better align item content with theory and better understand what participants are thinking while responding to these items.

Within-and between-person effects of screen-related needs and well-being

To further explore the links between psychological needs and well-being and reduce the risk of recall bias, we examined within-and between-person effects when people had used screens in the past hour. Within-and between-persons, our hypotheses were supported. Moving beyond commonly studied between-person effects, our within-person findings suggest that moments of higher overall psychological need satisfaction during screen time were related to moments of higher hedonic and eudaimonic well-being, even after controlling for the effect of weekend, time of day, and relevant sociodemographic factors. For positive affect, the impact of psychological needs during screen time at the within person level was stronger in the evening supporting past findings that show people might be better able to fulfill their needs during leisure time (Ryan et al., 2010). The R² s from these models showed these effects were practically meaningful (fixed effects R² .15-.24). These findings are consistent with daily data on social media needs (Van de Casteele et al., 2024), yet extend them to include hedonic and eudaimonic indicators of well-being.

Implications

Psychological need crafting interventions (van den Bogaard et al., 2024) could be tailored to screen time contexts to determine if students themselves can enhance their psychological needs while using screens. Moreover, as Van De Casteele (2024) suggested, mindfulness interventions could be examined as a means to enhance screen-related need experiences and their relationship with well-being.

Limitations and future directions

The data are self-report leading to social desirability or recall bias. Researchers should use direct measures of screen time (e.g., device measured screen time metrics). We were concerned that some participants might have claimed they did not use their device in order to avoid answering questions. A logistic mixed effects model showed that the odds of reporting being on screens at a given time point reduced over time, to a probability of 54.3%, (95% CI [.51, .57]) on the final survey compared to 71.4%, (95% CI [.69, .74]) on the first survey. To minimize participant burden, screen time duration and need frustration were not queried in the daily surveys and should be examined in future research. Although we intentionally assessed our variables at a broad level (i.e., overall screen time), it is possible that the variables operate differentially at different levels of specificity. For example, perceptions of need satisfaction and frustration while on social media may differ compared to while watching television. Moreover, Study 2 data were collected during restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, participants may have been using screen time differently to craft their psychological needs (Van de Casteele et al., 2024). Additionally, our findings may not generalize to other populations, particularly given the imbalance of females/women to males/men in our study and the lack of people identifying as non-binary. Since sex differences moderate the link between screen time and internalizing mental health symptoms (Tang et al., 2021), researchers should explore whether individuals of different sexes and/or genders have qualitatively different experiences during screen time, which may help explain variation in how screen time relates to well-being.

Research is needed in younger adolescents and young adults outside of university contexts to determine if these results are generalizable. Although we pre-registered the factor structures based on past studies (Holmquist et al., 2024; Tóth-Király et al., 2018 , 2019), these do not form an exhaustive list of possible factor structures, and we do not rule out that other alternatives (e.g., higher-order models) may be more suitable. Researchers have increasingly shown that affect might be best represented by different functions or types varying in in activation or arousal (Gilbert et al., 2008). Our measure of affect captured high arousal affect and may therefore omit low activation affect (e.g., contentment). Finally, we focused on well-being indicators and did not examine ill-being (e.g., symptoms of anxiety and depression). It is possible that people can both satisfy and frustrate their psychological needs in screen time and this would simultaneously impact both their ill-being and well-being.

Conclusions

Across two studies using a cross-sectional and experience sampling design, we showed that (1) a modified measure of screen-related psychological needs has valid and reliable scores and (2) screen-related psychological needs account for a significant proportion of variance in hedonic and eudaimonic well-being beyond screen time quantity. Our findings were particularly robust for the link between competence and well-being. Researchers are encouraged to continue investigating indicators of screen time quality to elucidate how screen time experiences impact overall well-being.

Declarations

Adjusted models included covariates of age, gender, parent's marital status, mother's education, and father's education. All models included a random intercept and random effects for Need SatisfactionWP, Need SatisfactionBP. In addition, the negative affect models included random effects for Is Weekend. The positive affect models included a random effect of daytime.

was modified by contextualizing the instructional stem to screen time and presenting a definition of screen time to participants (see OSF link). Items were rated on a scale of 1 (completely untrue) to 5 (completely true). Example satisfaction and frustration items, respectively, include "I feel capable at what I do" and "I feel insecure about my abilities (competence), "I feel my choices express who I really am" and "I feel pressured to do too many things (autonomy), and "I feel close and connected with other people who are important to me" and "I feel the relationships I have are just superficial" (relatedness). The original scale scores show good validity and reliability, and when items were modified to social media contexts demonstrated good reliability (alphas range .60-.83; Van de Casteele et al., 2023).

Psychological need satisfaction: One item from each subscale of the modified screenrelated psychological need satisfaction and frustration scale described above. To reduce burden, only satisfaction was assessed: competence satisfaction ("I felt capable at what I do"), autonomy satisfaction ("I felt that my decisions reflected what I really want"), relatedness satisfaction ("I felt connected with people who care for me, and for whom I care"). Participants responded based on how they felt when they last used a screen-based device for leisure. Items were selected based on the highest factor loading in a CFA (see pre-registration conference poster for details). A manifest variable representing psychological need satisfaction summed the autonomy, competence, and relatedness items.
